newsitem.title: USA: US debt on U.N. dues hampers peacekeeping plans.
newsitem.headline: US debt on U.N. dues hampers peacekeeping plans.

text.p: U.S. failure to pay the money it owes to the United Nations has hampered the Clinton administration's efforts to reshape international peacekeeping operations, the Washington Post reported in Sunday editions.

A draft State Department study, still subject to revision, concluded that U.S. arrearages of about $1.5 billion left the U.N. so cash-strapped that it had to borrow from peacekeeping budgets to cover day-to-day expenses, the Post said.

That meant the U.N. couldn't afford to pay for reforms that Washington believes are necessary to make peacekeeping operations better able to defuse regional conflicts such as those in Bosnia and parts of Africa.
Washington's influence with other U.N. members had also eroded, undermining U.S. efforts to reform peacekeeping operations.

"The financial crisis has undermined the ability of the United States and the United Nations to carry out some (peacekeeping) reforms," the paper quoted the study as saying. "Furthermore, given its role in the financial crisis, the United States is not a credible advocate for some financial reforms."

The report, a copy of which was obtained by the Washington Post, was prepared by the State Department's inspector general office as part of a review to assess how much progress had been made in implementing the administration's policy goals.

President Bill Clinton issued a directive in May 1994 listing a number of conditions for U.S. participation in peacekeeping operations, including whether an end was set to the operation and specifications that U.S. contributions might be in the form of logistics and transportations rather than troops.
The president also directed U.S. officials to pursue reforms, aimed at making international peacekeeping operations more effective and efficient.
